title: Party Spending & Campaign Finance
hook: Since Watergate, a law has capped how much a political party can spend directly coordinating with its own candidate. In 2026 the Supreme Court struck that cap down.
key_points: Post-Watergate campaign-finance law drew a line between a party's independent spending and spending coordinated with its candidate.
'Coordinated party expenditures' — money spent working directly with a candidate's campaign — were capped by federal law.
In June 2026 the Supreme Court struck down those limits, per NPR and SCOTUSblog.
Parties can now spend unlimited money coordinating directly with the candidates they support.
The ruling extends a decades-long trend of the Court loosening campaign-finance limits, from Buckley v. Valeo onward.
content_html: Campaign-finance law has long drawn a line between two kinds of party spending: money a party spends entirely on its own ("independent expenditures") and money it spends working directly with its candidate's campaign to buy ads or organize outreach ("coordinated expenditures"). Because coordinated spending functions almost like a direct contribution to the candidate, Congress capped it after Watergate to prevent parties from becoming a backdoor around individual contribution limits.
extra_html: In June 2026, the Supreme Court struck those caps down. NPR's Grady Martin reports the case centered on the post-Watergate law limiting how much a party can spend in direct coordination with its own candidates; SCOTUSblog confirmed the justices ruled against the limits. Writing in The Conversation, legal scholar John J. Martin notes the decision continues a pattern stretching back decades: since Buckley v. Valeo (1976) first distinguished contribution limits (upheld, to fight corruption) from expenditure limits (treated skeptically, as speech), the Court has steadily narrowed how much campaign spending government may restrict. The result: political parties can now spend unlimited sums coordinating directly with their candidates — reopening the very channel Congress once tried to cap. (This card describes U.S. campaign-finance law specifically; other democracies regulate party and candidate spending very differently.)

flashcards.prompt: What is the difference between 'independent' and 'coordinated' party campaign spending?
flashcards.back_html: Independent spending is a party acting entirely on its own; coordinated spending is done together with the candidate's campaign — which Congress capped because it resembles a direct contribution.

flashcards.prompt: What did the Supreme Court do to coordinated-spending limits in June 2026?

choices.text: Struck them down, letting parties spend unlimited amounts coordinating with candidates
Extended them to cover independent spending too

flashcards.explanation_html: The Court ruled against the post-Watergate caps, removing the limit on how much a party can spend working directly with its candidate.

flashcards.prompt: What broader trend does this 2026 ruling continue?

choices.text: Decades of the Court narrowing what campaign-spending limits government may impose
A trend of the Court expanding contribution limits
A move toward publicly funding all campaigns

flashcards.explanation_html: Since Buckley v. Valeo (1976), the Court has repeatedly struck down expenditure limits while treating them as protected speech.
